node.label: Jane Humphries
node.date_label: Enclosures, Common Rights, and Women (1990) · with Sara Horrell, Women’s Labour Force Participation (1995) · Childhood and Child Labour (2010) · The Lure of Aggregates (2013)
node.description: Jane Humphries places women’s and children’s work and fragile family economies at the centre of explanations of British industrialisation. Childhood and Child Labour in the British Industrial Revolution (2010) uses working men’s autobiographies to argue that industrialisation brought an upsurge in child labour, shaped by mechanization, large families and unreliable or absent breadwinners. With Sara Horrell, she studied women’s labour-force participation and the transition to the male-breadwinner family, 1790–1865 (1995). The Lure of Aggregates (2013) challenges Robert C. Allen’s high-wage interpretation for treating male earnings as a reliable measure of family wellbeing and offers cheap female and child labour as another stimulus to innovation. Reception includes a methodological dispute with Emma Griffin: Humphries questioned the causal account of breadwinner failure in Bread Winner (2020), while Griffin argued in a 2022 note that Humphries’s male-authored autobiographical sample could not sustain broad arguments about wider working-class experience.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Enclosures, Common Rights, and Women (1990); with Sara Horrell, Women’s Labour Force Participation and the Transition to the Male-Breadwinner Family, 1790–1865 (1995); Childhood and Child Labour in the British Industrial Revolution (2010); The Lure of Aggregates and the Pitfalls of the Patriarchal Perspective (2013; working paper 2011); with Benjamin Schneider, Spinning the Industrial Revolution (2019).
node.scope_note: The 2010 book was read only through publisher frontmatter and synopsis; main chapters remain unread. Selected 1995 article passages and selected pages of the 2011 working paper were read. The final 2013 articles and the 1990 article were read as abstracts only. The 2020 review and Griffin’s 2022 critical note supply the reception account. Referenced works by Pinchbeck, Berg, de Vries, Mokyr and Griffin were not independently read in full.

proposed_edges.relationship: In the 2011 working-paper version of ‘The Lure of Aggregates’, Humphries builds on Berg's The Age of Manufactures (1985; cited in the 1994 edition), quoting its finding that machines and processes were invented with female and child labour in mind, to explain innovation that bypassed artisan controls.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Oxford institutional working paper, July 2011, pp. 24–26 and associated notes read. Body text explicitly deploys Berg’s finding in its alternative account of innovation; n. 73 identifies the quotation as Berg, 1994 edition, p. 147. That edition and Berg’s other works were not independently read. The 2011 draft is not represented as the final 2013 article.
proposed_edges.map_label: Uses Berg on machinery and family labour (2011)

proposed_edges.relationship: In her review of Emma Griffin’s Bread Winner (2020), Humphries uses de Vries’s The Industrious Revolution (2008) on the value of domestic comforts to question whether rising male wages necessarily devalued homemakers’ contributions.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Open review’s argument and bibliography read. De Vries’s account is used to counter a specific household mechanism attributed to Griffin. The 2008 book is not independently read here; the relationship is this documented argumentative use in 2020.
proposed_edges.map_label: Uses de Vries on valued domestic labour (2020)

proposed_edges.relationship: In her review of Bread Winner (2020), Humphries uses Mokyr’s ‘More Work for Mother? Knowledge and Household Behavior, 1870–1945’ (2000) to explain how knowledge about infection increased the value of cleanliness and housework.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read in the body of Humphries’s open review immediately after the de Vries paragraph. This is a specific explanatory use within her objection to the devaluation hypothesis, not an inference from a reference list. Mokyr’s original article was not independently read for this packet.
proposed_edges.map_label: Uses Mokyr on knowledge and housework (2020)

proposed_edges.relationship: In ‘Enclosures, Common Rights, and Women’ (1990), Humphries argues that loss of common rights changed women’s position within families and increased families’ dependence on wages because women and children had been their principal users.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher abstract and original issue metadata read: Journal of Economic History 50(1), March 1990, pp. 17–42. Full article not read. Claim stays within the abstract’s stated argument; the online posting date of 2009 is not the original publication year.
proposed_edges.map_label: Connects common rights to women’s dependence (1990)

proposed_edges.relationship: In ‘Childhood and Child Labour in the British Industrial Revolution’ (2013), Humphries links an upsurge in children’s work to mechanization, work organization and vulnerable family economies, using working men’s autobiographies.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Abstract and issue metadata read: Economic History Review 66(2), May 2013, pp. 395–418; first online in 2012. This article is distinct from the 2010 monograph. Its body was not read; no independent audit of the autobiographical data is claimed.
proposed_edges.map_label: Explains the expansion of child labour (2013)

proposed_edges.relationship: In ‘The Lure of Aggregates and the Pitfalls of the Patriarchal Perspective’ (2013), Humphries criticizes the high-wage explanation of British industrialisation for treating male earnings as family welfare and proposes cheap female and child labour as an alternative stimulus to innovation.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Final article’s abstract and metadata read. The existing graph source already supports this bounded claim; reuse cd_humphries_2013. Selected passages in the separate 2011 working paper were also read. Do not conflate its pagination with pp. 693–714 of the final article. The existing field roster row is retained; there is no existing edge to duplicate.

proposed_edges.relationship: In ‘“…The Most Free From Objection …” The Sexual Division of Labor and Women's Work in Nineteenth-Century England’ (1987), Humphries contributes to women's history by arguing that the control of sexuality helped shape employment segregation, supplementing explanations based on childbearing and changes in production.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher abstract and issue metadata. The abstract identifies sexual control as an additional explanation for occupational segregation and says the argument is tested through regional correlations. The article body and statistical results remain unread; this edge records the stated intervention, without endorsing its causal inference. Women's history is an editorial field mapping to the documented argument about women's work. This work and endpoint pair are absent from the supplied input and from the earlier Humphries entry draft consulted for an additional duplicate check.
proposed_edges.map_label: Explains women's employment segregation through sexual control (1987)

proposed_edges.relationship: In ‘Careworn: The Economic History of Caring Labor’ (2024), Humphries contributes to quantitative history by using historical maintenance costs and commodity living costs to estimate paid domestic services, then imputing and aggregating the value of unpaid household labour.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher's open abstract, publication metadata and introduction through the paragraph beginning ‘In closing’. The introduction explains comparison of maintenance costs with a commodity basket, regression controls for heterogeneous evidence, and aggregation over households without domestic servants. Later empirical sections, tables and calculations were not audited. The claim concerns her stated estimation procedure, not the accuracy of its totals or adoption by other scholars. Quantitative history is an editorial mapping to this explicit historical estimation method; no claim that she founded the method or field is made.
proposed_edges.map_label: Estimates and aggregates unpaid domestic labour (2024)
